chapter_seo_title: RMJI Ch. 431: The Seven Iris Flower Trap & a Bone Hand from Nowhere
chapter_meta_description: The fake Seven Iris Flower is revealed as a demon snake’s crest. Han Li stays cold-eyed as the party takes heavy losses, but the real horror comes when a dead man walks—and a bone hand strikes from behind.
og_title: The Seven Iris Flower Was a Lie—And the Real Terror Came After
og_description: In chapter 431 of RMJI, the treasure hunters spring a brilliantly laid trap. The rainbow is venomous qi, the flower is a snake’s horn, and the skeleton beside the pool is a warning they didn’t read in time.
twitter_title: A fake treasure, a venomous snake, and a corpse that just won’t stay dead.
twitter_description: Han Li barely flinches as the party falls into an elaborate setup. The Seven Iris Flower was always a lie—and the final ambush hasn’t even begun.

lore_anchors.definition: A venomous spirit serpent whose fleshy head crest often marks its mutation level or poison sac. In *RMJI*, someone deliberately reshaped it into a flower bud as part of a trap.

A legendary multi-colored flower that glows with a miniature rainbow over its bloom. In this chapter, it is revealed as a completely fake lure—the rainbow is demonic qi, and the “flower” is a snake’s horn.

A weapon from a bygone age of cultivators, distinct from modern magic tools. They cannot be absorbed into the body but are far more powerful per use, making them highly coveted despite their lack of integration.

A legendary bamboo species whose wood can be refined into flying swords with innate lightning-attribute power. Han Li deliberately suppresses his Azure Bamboo Cloudswarm Swords’ Evil-Cleansing Divine Lightning to avoid revealing this origin material.
A lightning attribute imbued into the Azure Bamboo Cloudswarm Swords during refinement, explicitly suppressed by Han Li in this chapter to hide the swords’ material source.

cultural_notes_faq.q: Why did the Seven Iris Flower turn out to be a fake?
cultural_notes_faq.a: It was never a real spirit herb. Someone deliberately carved a Crested Snake’s horn into a flower shape and had the snake spray colored qi to mimic a rainbow—an elaborate trap luring treasure hunters into the venomous pool.

cultural_notes_faq.q: Why does Han Li suppress his sword’s lightning?
cultural_notes_faq.a: He does not want anyone to recognize that his Azure Bamboo Cloudswarm Swords are made from Divine Thunder Bamboo, a rare and valuable material that would immediately mark him as a target for theft or assassination.

cultural_notes_faq.q: What is the bone hand at the end of the chapter?
cultural_notes_faq.a: A skeletal hand pierces Hu Yue’s abdomen from behind, snatching a blue pill. It is almost certainly not the dead Jian—it might be a hidden puppet, a new enemy, or the trap-layer himself, still active in the cave.

Yes. Its green color resembles Han Li’s swords but carries faint black taint, suggesting it was refined with a dark or corrupted technique. This is almost certainly a clue about the cave’s true master and will likely be referenced again later.

cultural_notes_faq.q: How does this chapter reflect the “Mortal Stream” style?
cultural_notes_faq.a: It avoids heroic combat: Han Li stays passive, analyzes the trap, delivers a pinpoint assist, and then goes back to studying the evidence. The final attack is a cold, ambush-style kill, not a flashy duel—pure Dark Forest logic in execution.
